question: What is the main use of the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) in the ward?

options.A: To test the patient's long-term memory
options.B: To diagnose the exact cause of a brain injury
options.C: To check the strength of peripheral nerves
options.D: To measure a patient's level of consciousness

explanation: You'll use the GCS every day on clinical placement! It gives us a quick, reliable way to check and record how alert a patient is. You've got this! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why do nurses use numbers in the GCS instead of writing words like 'drowsy' in the patient's chart?

options.A: Doctors are not trained to read standard English descriptions
options.B: Words take too much time to write in a busy hospital chart
options.C: Numbers are the only way to bill insurance companies for care
options.D: Numerical scores prevent misunderstandings between different staff members

explanation: Words like 'drowsy' can mean different things to different nurses. A number gives everyone a clear, shared picture so we can easily track if the patient is getting better or worse. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT one of the three areas checked in the Glasgow Coma Scale?
explanation: Remember the three main parts of GCS: Eyes, Verbal, and Motor! Sensory touch isn't part of it. A handy trick for exams and the ward. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h2)

question: Which part of the Glasgow Coma Scale is usually seen as the best clue to how well a patient will recover?
explanation: The motor response checks deep brain pathways. It gives nurses and doctors the strongest clue about how a patient is recovering after a head injury. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h2)

question: What is the highest score a patient can get on the eye-opening part of the GCS?
explanation: Eye opening goes from 1 to 4. A score of 4 means the patient opens their eyes spontaneously without anyone touching or calling them! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h3)

question: A patient lies quietly with closed eyes, but opens them right away when you call their name loudly. What is their eye score?
explanation: Spot on! When they open their eyes only after you speak to them or call their name, that's a score of 3. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h3)

question: What is the maximum score for the verbal (talking) category in a fully alert adult?
explanation: The verbal score ranges from 1 to 5. Scoring a 5 means your patient is fully alert and oriented to time, place, and person. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h4)

question: How would you score a patient who speaks in full sentences, but insists they are in a different city and year?
explanation: Even though they are talking in sentences, getting the place and time wrong means they are confused. They get a verbal score of 4 for confused conversation. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h4)

question: What score do you give when a patient correctly follows simple commands, like squeezing your hand when asked?
explanation: Obeying commands is the highest motor score possible—a solid 6! It's always a relief to see a patient do this. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h5)

question: What is the main difference between decorticate and decerebrate posturing when scoring motor response?

options.A: Decorticate involves abnormal flexion inward, while decerebrate involves rigid extension outward
options.B: Decorticate affects only the legs, while decerebrate affects only the arms
options.C: Decorticate is scored as a 5, while decerebrate is scored as a 4
options.D: Decorticate means the patient obeys commands, while decerebrate means they make no sound

explanation: Think of decorticate (flexion/inward toward the core) scoring a 3, and decerebrate (extension/rigid outward) scoring a 2. Both point to serious brain stress, but knowing the physical posturing helps you chart accurately. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h5)

question: What is the lowest possible total score a patient can get on the Glasgow Coma Scale?
explanation: Since each of the three sections (Eyes, Verbal, Motor) has a minimum score of 1, the lowest total score possible is 3. (Even an unresponsive patient scores a 1 in each area!). [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h6)

question: At what total GCS score do clinicians usually start preparing to intubate and protect the patient's airway?
explanation: As nurses say in the emergency unit: 'Less than 8, intubate!' A score of 8 or lower usually means the patient can't protect their own airway. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h6)

question: What should you do if a patient cannot speak because they have an endotracheal breathing tube in their throat?

options.A: Score the patient with a verbal score of 1 for total silence
options.B: Give the patient a verbal score of 5 assuming they are normal
options.C: Document the verbal score as untestable and note the breathing tube
options.D: Leave the verbal score section completely blank on the chart

explanation: Never guess! When a physical barrier like a breathing tube stops you from testing, clearly document why you couldn't check it so other nurses understand. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h7)

question: A patient has severe swelling around both eyes from a facial injury, making it impossible for them to open their eyes. How should you document the eye score?

options.A: Force the eyelids open to check for a spontaneous score
options.B: Record a score of 4 because they might open them later
options.C: Record a score of 2 because swelling counts as pain
options.D: Note eye opening as untestable due to swelling

explanation: Never force swollen eyelids open! Always document that the eye score is untestable due to local trauma or edema, keeping your patient safe and comfortable. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T7#GNS222_U3_T7_h7)
